chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: Slow years, then Pee Wee Moore gets him a trial with Louis Jordan's big band
summary: After a drifting 1950-51, baritone player Pee Wee Moore tells him Jordan's new 14-piece band needs a pianist, and he plays one night on trial.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: But I came back to Washington, and it was another thing of gigging around, a date here with this group or that group, or maybe making up one of my own for a week or a couple of weeks or so. And things got kind of slow from the period of, say, 1950 through about the latter part of 1951. I mean, I wasn't doing anything that pointed in any direction.

In 1951, I was not working. I think it was in October 1951. I was home, and I got this call from a friend of mine that I had known. I'd just met him previously... I don't remember really where I had met him. But this fellow's name

was Newmore(?) Moore, and everyone called him Pee Wee -- Pee Wee Moore. He was a baritone saxophone player who later played with the Dizzy Gillespie Band. He called me and said that he was working with Louis Jordan's band. Well, up until that period, I had always known Louis Jordan to have a quintet that he called The Tympany Five, and I was wondering, because he never used a baritone saxophone player. So I said, "What's happening?" "Well, Louis has a big band. It had something like 14 pieces, and the pianist had just quit or been fired in Atlanta, Georgia, and the band had been without a pianist for about three or four days. So he asked me if I would come up that night to where I'd been playing.

Right now I don't remember exactly where they were playing that night. But I went up and talked to Louis Jordan, and he said, "You can make tonight -- we don't have a pianist. And we'll talk about it afterwards." So I went up and I made that night, which was a Saturday night. After the date that night, Louis paid me off, and I asked him what did he think. He says, "Well, I've got to go to New York over the weekend, and I'll be back Monday, and I'll tell you what I think."
